section.heading: 2.8. The Derivative as a Function
The Derivative Function
section.paragraph: In the preceding section we considered the derivative of a function $$f$$ at a fixed number $$a$$ :
$$f^{\prime}(a) = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{f(a + h) - f(a)}{h}$$
Here we change our point of view and let the number $$a$$ vary. If we replace $$a$$ in Equation 1 by a variable $$x$$ , we obtain
$$f^{\prime}(x) = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{h}$$

Given any number $$x$$ for which this limit exists, we assign to $$x$$ the number $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ . So we can regard $$f^{\prime}$$ as a new function, called the derivative of $$\mathbf{f}$$ and defined by Equation 2. We know that the value of $$f^{\prime}$$ at $$x$$ , $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ , can be interpreted geometrically as the slope of the tangent line to the graph of $$f$$ at the point $$\left( x,f(x) \right)$$ .

The function $$f^{\prime}$$ is called the derivative of $$f$$ because it has been “derived” from $$f$$ by the limiting operation in Equation 2. The domain of $$f^{\prime}$$ is the set $$\left\{ x \middle| f^{\prime}(x){exists} \right\}$$ and may be smaller than the domain of $$f$$ .

example.paragraph: The slope of the tangent drawn at $$A$$ appears to be about $$- 1$$ , so we plot the point $$A^{\prime}$$ with a $$y$$ -value of $$- 1$$ on the graph of $$f^{\prime}$$ (directly beneath $$A$$ ). The tangents at $$B$$ and $$D$$ are horizontal, so the derivative is $$0$$ there and the graph of $$f^{\prime}$$ crosses the $$x$$ -axis (where $$y = 0$$ ) at the points $$B^{\prime}$$ and $$D^{\prime}$$ , directly beneath $$B$$ and $$D$$ . Between $$B$$ and $$D$$ , the graph of $$f$$ is steepest at $$C$$ and the tangent line there appears to have slope $$1$$ , so the largest value of $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ between $$B^{\prime}$$ and $$D^{\prime}$$ is $$1$$ (at $$C^{\prime}$$ ).

Notice that between $$B$$ and $$D$$ the tangents have positive slope, so $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ is positive there. (The graph of $$f^{\prime}$$ is above the $$x$$ -axis.) But to the right of $$D$$ the tangents have negative slope, so $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ is negative there. (The graph of $$f^{\prime}$$ is below the $$x$$ -axis.)

example.heading: Example 2

list.item: (a) If $$f(x) = x^{3} - x$$ , find a formula for $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ .
(b) Illustrate this formula by comparing the graphs of $$f$$ and $$f^{\prime}$$ .

example.paragraph: Solution

list.item: (a) When using Equation 2 to compute a derivative, we must remember that the variable is $$h$$ and that $$x$$ is temporarily regarded as a constant during the calculation of the limit. $$\begin{array}{l} {{f^{\prime}(x)} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}{\frac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{h} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{{\lbrack{{({x + h})}^{3} - {({x + h})}}\rbrack} - {\lbrack{x^{3} - x}\rbrack}}{h}}}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}(x)} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{x^{3} + 3x^{2}h + 3xh^{2} + h^{3} - x - h - x^{3} + x}{h}}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}(x)} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{3x^{2}h + 3xh^{2} + h^{3} - h}{h}}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}(x)} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}{({3x^{2} + 3xh + h^{2} - 1})} = 3x^{2} - 1}} \end{array}$$

(b) We use a calculator to graph $$f$$ and $$f^{\prime}$$ in Figure 3. Notice that $$f^{\prime}(x) = 0$$ when $$f$$ has horizontal tangents and $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ is positive when the tangents have positive slope. So these graphs serve as a check on our work in part (a). example.heading: Example 3
example.paragraph: If $$f(x) = \sqrt{x}$$ , find the derivative of $$f$$ . State the domain of $$f^{\prime}$$ .
Solution

$$\begin{array}{l} {{f^{\prime}{(x)}} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{h}} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{\sqrt{x + h} - \sqrt{x}}{h}}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}{(x)}} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\left( {\frac{\sqrt{x + h} - \sqrt{x}}{h} \cdot \frac{\sqrt{x + h} + \sqrt{x}}{\sqrt{x + h} + \sqrt{x}}} \right) {({{Rationalize the numerator}.})}}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}{(x)}} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}{\frac{{({x + h})} - x}{h({\sqrt{x + h} + \sqrt{x}})} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{h}{h({\sqrt{x + h} + \sqrt{x}})}}}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}{(x)}} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}{\frac{1}{\sqrt{x + h} + \sqrt{x}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{x} + \sqrt{x}} = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}}}}} \end{array}$$

We see that $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ exists if $$x > 0$$ , so the domain of $$f^{\prime}$$ is $$\left( {0,\infty} \right)$$ . This is slightly smaller than the domain of $$f$$ , which is $$\lbrack 0,\infty)$$ .

section.paragraph: Let’s check to see that the result of Example 3 is reasonable by looking at the graphs of $$f$$ and $$f^{\prime}$$ in Figure 4. When $$x$$ is close to $$0$$ , $$\sqrt{x}$$ is also close to $$0$$ , so $$f^{\prime}(x) = 1 \slash \left( 2\sqrt{x} \right)$$ is very large and this corresponds to the steep tangent lines near $$(0,0)$$ in Figure 4(a) and the large values of $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ just to the right of $$0$$ in Figure 4(b). When $$x$$ is large, $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ is very small and this corresponds to the flatter tangent lines at the far right of the graph of $$f$$ and the horizontal asymptote of the graph of $$f^{\prime}$$ .

example.heading: Example 4
example.paragraph: Find $$f^{\prime}$$ if $$f(x) = \frac{1 - x}{2 + x}$$ .
Solution

$$\begin{array}{l} {{f^{\prime}{(x)}} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{f(x + h) - f(x)}{h}}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}{(x)}} = {\underset{h\rightarrow 0}{\lim}\frac{\frac{1 - {({x + h})}}{2 + {({x + h})}} - \frac{1 - x}{2 + x}}{h}}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}{(x)}} = {\underset{h\rightarrow 0}{\lim}\frac{{({1 - x - h})}{({2 + x})} - {({1 - x})}{({2 + x + h})}}{h({2 + x + h})({2 + x})}}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}(x)} = {\underset{h\rightarrow 0}{\lim}\frac{{({2 - x - 2h - x^{2} - xh})} - {({2 - x + h - x^{2} - xh})}}{h({2 + x + h})({2 + x})}}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}(x)} = {\underset{h\rightarrow 0}{\lim}\frac{- 3h}{h({2 + x + h})({2 + x})}}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}(x)} = \underset{h\rightarrow 0}{\lim}\frac{- 3}{({2 + x + h}){({2 + x})}} = - \frac{3}{{({2 + x})}^{2}}} \end{array}$$

section.heading: Other Notations
section.paragraph: If we use the traditional notation $$y = f(x)$$ to indicate that the independent variable is $$x$$ and the dependent variable is $$y$$ , then some common alternative notations for the derivative are as follows:
$$f^{\prime}(x) = y^{\prime} = \frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}} = \frac{\mathit{df}}{\mathit{dx}} = \frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}f(x) = Df(x) = D_{x}f(x)$$
The symbols $$D$$ and $$d \slash dx$$ are called differentiation operators because they indicate the operation of differentiation, which is the process of calculating a derivative.

The symbol $$dy \slash dx$$ , which was introduced by Leibniz, should not be regarded as a ratio (for the time being); it is simply a synonym for $$f^{\prime}(x)$$ . Nonetheless, it is a very useful and suggestive notation, especially when used in conjunction with increment notation. Referring to Equation 2.7.6, we can rewrite the definition of derivative in Leibniz notation in the form
$$\frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}} = \lim\limits_{\Delta x\rightarrow 0}\frac{\Delta y}{\Delta x}$$
If we want to indicate the value of a derivative $$dy \slash dx$$ in Leibniz notation at a specific number $$a$$ , we use the notation
$$\left. \frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}} \right|_{x = a}$$
or
$$\left. \frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}} \right\rbrack_{x = a}$$
which is a synonym for $$f^{\prime}(a)$$ . The vertical bar means “evaluate at.”

note.title: Definition
note.heading: Definition
note.paragraph: A function $$f$$ is differentiable at $$\mathbf{a}$$ if $$f^{\prime}(a)$$ exists. It is differentiable on an open interval $$(a,b)$$ [or $$(a,\infty)$$ or $$( - \infty,a)$$ or $$( - \infty,\infty)$$ ] if it is differentiable at every number in the interval.

example.heading: Example 5
example.paragraph: Where is the function $$\left. f(x) = \middle| x \right|$$ differentiable?

Solution If $$x > 0$$ , then $$\left| x \middle| = x \right.$$ and we can choose $$h$$ small enough that $$x + h > 0$$ and hence $$\left| x + h \middle| = x + h \right.$$ . Therefore, for $$x > 0$$ , we have

$$\begin{array}{l} {{f^{\prime}(x)} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{\left| x + h \middle| - \middle| x \right|}{h} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{\left( {x + h} \right) - x}{h}}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}(x)} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{h}{h} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}1 = 1}} \end{array}$$
and so $$f$$ is differentiable for any $$x > 0$$ .

Similarly, for $$x < 0$$ we have $$\left| x \middle| = - x \right.$$ and $$h$$ can be chosen small enough that $$x + h < 0$$ and so $$\left| x + h \middle| = - \left( {x + h} \right) \right.$$ . Therefore, for $$x < 0$$ ,

$$\begin{array}{l} {{f^{\prime}(x)} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{\left| x + h \middle| - \middle| x \right|}{h} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{- \left( {x + h} \right) - \left( {- x} \right)}{h}}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}(x)} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{- h}{h} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\left( {- 1} \right) = - 1}} \end{array}$$
and so $$f$$ is differentiable for any $$x < 0$$ .
For $$x = 0$$ we have to investigate

$$\begin{array}{l} {{f^{\prime}(0)} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{f\left( {0 + h} \right) - f(0)}{h}}} \\ {\phantom{f^{\prime}(0)} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{\left| 0 + h \middle| - \middle| 0 \right|}{h} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{|h|}{h} ({if it exists})}} \end{array}$$
Let’s compute the left and right limits separately:
$$\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0^{+}}\frac{|h|}{h} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0^{+}}\frac{h}{h} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0^{+}}1 = 1$$
and
$$\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0^{-}}\frac{|h|}{h} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0^{-}}\frac{- h}{h} = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0^{-}}\left( {- 1} \right) = - 1$$
Since these limits are different, $$f^{\prime}(0)$$ does not exist. Thus $$f$$ is differentiable at all $$x$$ except $$0$$ .
A formula for $$f^{\prime}$$ is given by
$$f^{\prime}(x) = \begin{cases} 1 & {{if}x > 0} \\ {- 1} & {{if}x < 0} \end{cases}$$

and its graph is shown in Figure 5(b). The fact that $$f^{\prime}(0)$$ does not exist is reflected geometrically in the fact that the curve $$\left. y = \middle| x \right|$$ does not have a tangent line at $$(0,0)$$ . [See Figure 5(a).]

section.paragraph: Both continuity and differentiability are desirable properties for a function to have. The following theorem shows how these properties are related.

note.title: Theorem
note.heading: Theorem
note.paragraph: If $$f$$ is differentiable at $$a$$ , then $$f$$ is continuous at $$a$$ .

note.title: Proof
note.heading: Proof
note.paragraph: To prove that $$f$$ is continuous at $$a$$ , we have to show that $$\lim_{x\rightarrow a}f(x) = f(a)$$ . We will do this by showing that the difference $$f(x) - f(a)$$ approaches $$0$$ .
The given information is that $$f$$ is differentiable at $$a$$ , that is,
An important aspect of problem solving is trying to find a connection between the given and the unknown. See Step 2 (Think of a Plan) in Principles of Problem Solving following Chapter 1.
exists (see Equation 2.7.5). To connect the given and the unknown, we divide and multiply $$f(x) - f(a)$$ by $$x - a$$ (which we can do when $$x \neq a$$ ):
Thus, using Limit Law 4, we can write

$$\begin{array}{l} {{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}\left\lbrack {f(x) - f(a)} \right\rbrack} = {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}\frac{f(x) - f(a)}{x - a}{({x - a})}}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}\left\lbrack {f(x) - f(a)} \right\rbrack} = {\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}\frac{f(x) - f(a)}{x - a} \cdot \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}{({x - a})}}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}\left\lbrack {f(x) - f(a)} \right\rbrack} = {f^{\prime}(a) \cdot 0 = 0}} \end{array}$$
To use what we have just proved, we start with $$f(x)$$ and add and subtract $$f(a)$$ :

$$\begin{array}{l} {{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}f(x)} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}{\lbrack{f(a) + (f(x) - f(a)})\rbrack}} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}f(x)} = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}f(a) + \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}\left\lbrack {f(x) - f(a)} \right\rbrack} \\ {\phantom{\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}f(x)} = {f(a) + 0 = f(a)}} \end{array}$$

section.paragraph: NOTE The converse of Theorem 4 is false; that is, there are functions that are continuous but not differentiable. For instance, the function $$\left. f(x) = \middle| x \right|$$ is continuous at $$0$$ because
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0}f(x) = \lim\limits_{x\rightarrow 0}|x| = 0 = f(0)$$
(See Example 2.3.7.) But in Example 5 we showed that $$f$$ is not differentiable at $$0$$ .
section.heading: How Can a Function Fail to Be Differentiable?
section.paragraph: We saw that the function $$\left. y = \middle| x \right|$$ in Example 5 is not differentiable at $$0$$ and Figure 5(a) shows that its graph changes direction abruptly when $$x = 0$$ . In general, if the graph of a function $$f$$ has a “corner” or “kink” in it, then the graph of $$f$$ has no tangent at this point and $$f$$ is not differentiable there. [In trying to compute $$f^{\prime}(a)$$ , we find that the left and right limits are different.]

Theorem 4 gives another way for a function not to have a derivative. It says that if $$f$$ is not continuous at $$a$$ , then $$f$$ is not differentiable at $$a$$ . So at any discontinuity (for instance, a jump discontinuity) $$f$$ fails to be differentiable.
A third possibility is that the curve has a vertical tangent line when $$x = a$$ ; that is, $$f$$ is continuous at $$a$$ and
$$\lim\limits_{x\rightarrow a}|f^{\prime}(x)| = \infty$$

This means that the tangent lines become steeper and steeper as $$\left. x\rightarrow a \right.$$ . Figure 6 shows one way that this can happen; Figure 7(c) shows another. Figure 7 illustrates the three possibilities that we have discussed.

section.heading: Higher Derivatives
section.paragraph: If $$f$$ is a differentiable function, then its derivative $$f^{\prime}$$ is also a function, so $$f^{\prime}$$ may have a derivative of its own, denoted by $$\left( f^{\prime} \right)^{\prime} = f^{''}$$ . This new function $$f^{''}$$ is called the second derivative of $$f$$ because it is the derivative of the derivative of $$f$$ . Using Leibniz notation, we write the second derivative of $$y = f(x)$$ as

$$\underset{\begin{matrix} {derivative} \\ {of} \end{matrix}}{\underset{︸}{\frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}}}\underset{\begin{matrix} {first} \\ {derivative} \end{matrix}}{\underset{︸}{\left( \frac{\mathit{dy}}{\mathit{dx}} \right)}} = \underset{\begin{matrix} {second} \\ {derivative} \end{matrix}}{\underset{︸}{\frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}}}}$$

example.heading: Example 6
example.paragraph: If $$f(x) = x^{3} - x$$ , find and interpret $$f^{''}(x)$$ .
Solution In Example 2 we found that the first derivative is $$f^{\prime}(x) = 3x^{2} - 1$$ . So the second derivative is

$$\begin{array}{l} {{f^{''}(x)} = {{(f^{\prime})}^{\prime}(x) = \lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{f^{\prime}(x + h) - f^{\prime}(x)}{h}}} \\ {\phantom{{f^{''}(x)} = {{(f^{\prime})}^{\prime}(x)}} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{{\lbrack{3{({x + h})}^{2} - 1}\rbrack} - {\lbrack{3x^{2} - 1}\rbrack}}{h}}} \\ {\phantom{{f^{''}(x)} = {{(f^{\prime})}^{\prime}(x)}} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}\frac{3x^{2} + 6xh + 3h^{2} - 1 - 3x^{2} + 1}{h}}} \\ {\phantom{{f^{''}(x)} = {{(f^{\prime})}^{\prime}(x)}} = {\lim\limits_{h\rightarrow 0}{({6x + 3h})} = 6x}} \end{array}$$
The graphs of $$f$$ , $$f^{\prime}$$ , and $$f^{''}$$ are shown in Figure 10.

example.paragraph: We can interpret $$f^{''}(x)$$ as the slope of the curve $$y = f^{\prime}(x)$$ at the point $$\left( {x,f^{\prime}(x)} \right)$$ . In other words, it is the rate of change of the slope of the original curve $$y = f(x)$$ .

Notice from Figure 10 that $$f^{''}(x)$$ is negative when $$y = f^{\prime}(x)$$ has negative slope and positive when $$y = f^{\prime}(x)$$ has positive slope. So the graphs serve as a check on our calculations.

section.paragraph: In general, we can interpret a second derivative as a rate of change of a rate of change. The most familiar example of this is acceleration, which we define as follows.
If $$s = s(t)$$ is the position function of an object that moves in a straight line, we know that its first derivative represents the velocity $$\upsilon(t)$$ of the object as a function of time:
$$\upsilon(t) = s^{\prime}(t) = \frac{ds}{\mathit{dt}}$$

The instantaneous rate of change of velocity with respect to time is called the acceleration $$a(t)$$ of the object. Thus the acceleration function is the derivative of the velocity function and is therefore the second derivative of the position function:
$$a(t) = \upsilon^{\prime}(t) = s^{''}(t)$$
or, in Leibniz notation,
$$a = \frac{d\upsilon}{\mathit{dt}} = \frac{d^{2}s}{dt^{2}}$$
Acceleration is the change in velocity you feel when speeding up or slowing down in a car.

The third derivative $$f^{'''}$$ is the derivative of the second derivative: $$f^{'''} = \left( f^{''} \right)^{\prime}$$ . So $$f^{'''}(x)$$ can be interpreted as the slope of the curve $$y = f^{''}(x)$$ or as the rate of change of $$f^{''}(x)$$ . If $$y = f(x)$$ , then alternative notations for the third derivative are
$$y^{'''} = f^{'''}(x) = \frac{d}{\mathit{dx}}\left( \frac{d^{2}y}{dx^{2}} \right) = \frac{d^{3}y}{dx^{3}}$$

We can also interpret the third derivative physically in the case where the function is the position function $$s = s(t)$$ of an object that moves along a straight line. Because $$s^{'''} = {(s^{''})}^{\prime} = a^{\prime}$$ , the third derivative of the position function is the derivative of the acceleration function and is called the jerk:
$$j = \frac{da}{\mathit{dt}} = \frac{d^{3}s}{dt^{3}}$$
Thus the jerk $$j$$ is the rate of change of acceleration. It is aptly named because a large jerk means a sudden change in acceleration, which causes an abrupt movement.

section.paragraph: We have seen that one application of second and third derivatives occurs in analyzing the motion of objects using acceleration and jerk. We will investigate another application of second derivatives in Section 4.3, where we show how knowledge of $$f^{''}$$ gives us information about the shape of the graph of $$f$$ . In Chapter 11 we will see how second and higher derivatives enable us to represent functions as sums of infinite series.
